module_title: Section 358 BNS, BNSS Overlaps, and the General Clauses Act
introduction: This intermediate tier drives into the exact statutory provisions that manage the transition. It covers the specific 'Repeal and Savings' sections of the new codes, the role of the General Clauses Act, and the complex hybrid scenarios where old crimes meet new procedures.

core_concepts.title: Repeal and Savings (Sec 358 BNS, Sec 531 BNSS, Sec 170 BSA)
core_concepts.description:
These are the final sections of the new codes that officially 'repeal' (cancel) the IPC, CrPC, and IEA.
- The 'Savings' Proviso: These sections explicitly state that the repeal shall not affect the previous operation of the old codes. Any right, privilege, obligation, or liability acquired, accrued, or incurred under the old codes remains legally alive.

core_concepts.title: Section 6 of the General Clauses Act, 1897
core_concepts.description: When a central act is repealed, Section 6 of the General Clauses Act automatically steps in to prevent legal chaos. It dictates that unless a different intention appears, the repeal shall not affect any investigation, legal proceeding, or remedy regarding any past right or punishment. The new Sanhitas explicitly invoke this principle.

core_concepts.title: The Hybrid Scenario: Old Crime, New FIR
core_concepts.description:
What happens if an IPC crime (e.g., committed in 2023) is reported *after* July 1, 2024?
- Substantive Law: The FIR will be registered under the **IPC** (e.g., Sec 420 for cheating).
- Procedural Law: Since the investigation itself is initiating *after* July 1, the police will use the **BNSS** procedures (e.g., digital search/seizure, 14-day preliminary enquiry) and the **BSA** rules for evidence collection. This creates a hybrid legal environment.

core_concepts.title: BNSS Transition: Trials vs. Investigations
core_concepts.description:
Section 531 of BNSS is tricky:
- If an appeal, application, trial, inquiry, or investigation was already *pending* right before July 1, 2024, it must be disposed of according to the **CrPC**.
- Therefore, a trial that started in June 2024 cannot suddenly start using BNSS's 'Trial in Absentia' rules in August.

important_entities.name: Substantive Law vs. Procedural Law
important_entities.key_fact: Substantive is strictly prospective; Procedural is generally retrospective (unless saved).
important_entities.significance: Substantive law (BNS/IPC) defines the crime and punishment. It CANNOT apply retrospectively. Procedural law (BNSS/CrPC) defines the process. Procedural laws *can* apply to old crimes, but Section 531 of BNSS explicitly 'saves' pending CrPC matters to avoid disrupting ongoing trials.

trap_alerts_and_exceptions.explanation: If a crime happened in 2018, but the FIR is lodged on July 5, 2024, an examiner might trick you by saying: 'Because the crime is governed by IPC, the investigation must be governed by CrPC.' **FALSE**. Because the investigation had not 'commenced/pending' before July 1, the new BNSS procedure applies to this old IPC crime.

mnemonics_and_tricks.explanation: Always look to the very last section of each new code to find the transitional rules.

exam_strategy_tips: If a Judiciary question asks 'Under which statutory principle do pending IPC cases survive the enactment of the BNS?', you MUST cite **Section 358 of BNS** read with **Section 6 of the General Clauses Act, 1897**.
